introduction: The primary aim was to test the preliminary effectiveness of a live online exercise program led by qualified instructors on older adults’ physical activity levels, compared with a waitlist control group.
methodology: Pilot convergent parallel mixed-methods RCT. Community-dwelling women and men aged 65 to 80 were randomized to an 8-week live online exercise program delivered on Zoom (ACTIVE) or a waitlist control (CON). Data came from an accelerometer, questionnaires and interviews. Pre-to-post changes were analyzed with a two-way repeated measures ANOVA; interviews were thematically analyzed in Dedoose.
theory: Guided by the CONSORT 2010 statement: extension for pilot and feasibility trials. No theory is named.
results: In the ACTIVE group, depressive symptoms decreased pre to post intervention (interaction p = 0.012) and life-space mobility increased (interaction p = 0.014). There were no significant between- or within-group differences for anxiety or loneliness, and no between-group differences in daily steps or nutrition risk. Attendance was 97% in the ACTIVE group.
discussion: The authors report that the program did not affect habitual physical activity but reduced depressive symptoms and improved life-space mobility, with excellent adherence and acceptability. They describe online exercise programs as viable service-delivery options, particularly when in-person programming is unavailable.
limitations: The authors acknowledge a small sample, which left the pilot underpowered for its primary outcome, and a lack of blinding of assessors and participants. They note the sample included only English-speaking people with home internet access. They suggest future studies include marginalized populations and different language options, including subtitles.

introduction.q: The primary objective of this pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT) was to determine the preliminary effectiveness of a live online exercise program from qualified instructors on older adults’ levels of PA compared to a waitlist control group.

methodology.q: This pilot convergent parallel mixed-methods RCT was guided by the CONSORT 2010 statement: extension for pilot and feasibility trials
Older community-dwelling women and men between the ages of 65 and 80 were recruited from Hamilton, Ontario, and the surrounding area.
A convenience sample size of 32 participants is aligned with previous online exercise pilot studies
Thirty-three older women and men participated in this study.
Participants underwent an 8-week intervention consisting of thrice-weekly 60-minute online exercise classes (totalling 24 exercise classes) delivered online via Zoom.
Habitual PA levels were the primary outcomes and were assessed using the armband BodyMedia Sensewear Pro II accelerometer
methodology.loc: Materials and methods, Quantitative data collection, Physical activity

methodology.q: Questionnaires were administered online using LimeSurvey
The Geriatric Depression Scale Short Form (GDS-SF) assesses depressive symptoms using 15 questions
Pre-to-post-intervention changes in quantitative outcome measures were analyzed using a two-way repeated measures ANOVA
Semi-structured, open-ended 1:1 interviews were conducted and audio recorded via Zoom
methodology.loc: Materials and methods, Qualitative data collection

methodology.q: Semi-structured interviews were thematically analyzed using the computer software Dedoose Version 9.0.17

theory.q: This pilot convergent parallel mixed-methods RCT was guided by the CONSORT 2010 statement: extension for pilot and feasibility trials

results.q: We observed an interaction (p = 0.012) for the Geriatric Depression Scale where the ACTIVE group decreased from pre-to-post intervention
We observed an interaction (p = 0.014) for life-space mobility where the ACTIVE group increased from pre-to-post intervention
There were no differences between groups for daily steps and daily active energy expenditure measured by the accelerometer following the intervention compared to the CON
There were no significant between or within-group differences for symptoms of anxiety and loneliness
There were no between-group differences in nutrition risk
Attendance rates were 97% in the ACTIVE group
Overall, participants reported being either satisfied or very satisfied with the intervention 98% of the time.
Five overarching themes and eight sub-themes were identified related to perceptions, experiences, and feasibility of the program.

discussion.q: The program did not affect participants’ habitual PA levels but reduced depressive symptoms, improved life-space mobility, and had excellent adherence and acceptability.

Online exercise programs are viable service-delivery options, particularly when in-person programming is unavailable due to physical distance, space limitations, and/or public health measures encouraging reduced mobility to slow viral spread.

limitations.q: There are several limitations with our study; however, primarily, we acknowledge the small sample size.
The study was a pilot and, therefore, underpowered to determine if there was an interaction for our primary outcome.
Another limitation of the study includes a lack of blinding for our assessors and participants to group allocation.
Our study only included English-speaking individuals with internet access at home with a tablet, computer, or phone.
Future studies should attempt to include marginalized populations to improve generalizability with different language options, including subtitles.

abstract_claims.q: Exercise reduces these risks, but older adults have low levels of participation in physical activity and exercise.
participants in the ACTIVE group reported reduced symptoms of depression
The ACTIVE group had good adherence (97%) and acceptability (98%).

Five themes were identified, including (1) Feasibility of the online exercise program; (2) Perceived health benefits and improvements; (3) Registered Kinesiologists and Physiotherapists contributed to perceived safety; (4) Social connectivity associated with synchronous/live delivery; and (5) Growing old gracefully and preventing disability.
Our online exercise program was acceptable to older adults, had good adherence, reduced depression, and increased life space.
Participants reported improved functional and mental health benefits.
Further research is warranted to expand on these findings.
